Thank you for the clear summary—I’m feeling a lot more comfortable with the plan now. I do have a few quick questions before we go ahead:

1. **Medication list / blood thinners** – I’m on a daily **warfarin** for my atrial fibrillation and a **metformin** for my diabetes, plus a **lisinopril** for blood pressure and an **inhaled albuterol‑ipratropium** combo for my COPD. Will any of these need to be held before the endoscopy or surgery, and when can I restart them afterward?

2. **Anesthesia details** – You mentioned lung‑protective ventilation and a bronchodilator before the case. Will I be given a short‑acting steroid or anything else for my COPD on the day of the procedure?

3. **Post‑procedure diet** – After a successful endoscopic removal, you said clear liquids can start 4–6 hours later. If I’m still a little nauseated, is it okay to start with something like ginger tea or plain crackers, or should I wait until the full 6 hours?

4. **Signs to watch for while I’m waiting** – Besides vomiting, fever, worsening pain, or no gas, is there anything else (e.g., swelling of the legs, shortness of breath) that I should call the team about right away?

5. **Follow‑up labs** – Will I need any blood work (e.g., blood‑sugar checks, kidney labs) before I’m discharged, or will those be done only if something changes?

6. **Physical activity** – After I’m cleared to go home, is light walking around the house fine the day after discharge, or should I rest completely for the first 24 hours?

I appreciate the thoroughness of the plan and just want to make sure I’m doing everything right. Thank you!

Below are the practical answers to each of your questions. I’ve organized them the same way you asked so it’s easy to follow. --- ## 1. Medication list / blood thinners | Medication | What we do before the procedure | When we restart it | Why | |------------|--------------------------------|--------------------|-----| | **Warfarin** (daily) | **Held** the evening before the endoscopy or surgery (≈ 12–14 h before). If the case is *only* an endoscopic removal, many centers give a **single dose of low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH)** on the morning of the procedure to protect against clot formation while the warfarin is off. For a laparoscopic operation we usually **hold warfarin** and give LMWH as “bridge” therapy. | • Endoscopy: Restart warfarin **the evening of the procedure** (or the next morning) **if there is no significant bleeding**.
• Laparoscopy: Restart **24 h after surgery** once the surgeon confirms the wound is dry, again **if there is no bleeding**. LMWH is stopped once warfarin is therapeutic again (INR ≈ 2‑3). | Warfarin increases bleeding risk. Holding it reduces that risk, and the short‑acting LMWH covers you against clot formation while your INR falls. | | **Metformin** (diabetes) | **Held the morning of the procedure** (about 6‑8 h before). This is standard for any case that involves fasting or anesthesia because metformin can increase the risk of lactic acidosis when kidneys receive less blood flow. | **Restart** once you are eating and your blood‑glucose is stable (usually **the same day** after you tolerate a regular meal). If you are still NPO after the procedure, you can start a **low‑dose sliding‑scale insulin** (the nursing team will arrange it) and re‑introduce metformin later that day or the next morning. | Prevents lactic acidosis in the setting of peri‑operative dehydration or reduced kidney perfusion. | | **Lisinopril** (blood pressure) | **Held the morning of the case** (the dose you would normally take that morning). ACE inhibitors can cause a transient drop in blood pressure when you’re under anesthesia and can blunt the body’s response to low‑volume states. | **Resume** once you are awake, hemodynamically stable, and able to take oral meds (usually **the night of the procedure** or the next morning). | Reduces intra‑operative hypotension. | | **Albuterol‑Ipratropium inhaler** (COPD) | **Continue** right up to the time of the case. Use it **just before arriving to the pre‑operative area** (a puff or two) and again **immediately after emergence from anesthesia** if you feel wheezy. | Continue **as usual** after the procedure; you may be asked to use it more frequently for the first 24 h while the lungs recover from the anesthesia effects. | Maintains airway patency; no need to stop. | > **Bottom line:** > • Warfarin and lisinopril are held on the day of the procedure (warfarin is “bridged” with LMWH). > • Metformin is held the morning of the case and restarted once you tolerate food. > • Your inhaler stays on — use it right before you go to the OR and after you wake up. --- ## 2. Anesthesia details for your COPD * **Bronchodilator pre‑medication** – You will receive a **nebulized albuterol (or a metered‑dose inhaler puff)** just before induction, plus the ipratropium you already use. * **Short‑acting steroid** – Many anesthesiologists give a **single dose of IV methylprednisolone (e.g., 40 mg)** for patients with moderate‑to‑severe COPD to reduce airway inflammation and the risk of post‑operative bronchospasm. We will confirm that with you; if you have never taken a systemic steroid before, we’ll explain the brief dose and its benefits. * **Lung‑protective ventilation** – Tidal volume ≈ 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight, a slightly higher respiratory rate, and a modest positive‑end‑expiratory pressure (PEEP) to keep alveoli open. * **Monitoring** – Continuous ECG, pulse‑oximetry, capnography, and blood‑pressure monitoring. The anesthesia team will also watch your **INR** (for the warfarin) and give **reversal agents** (vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate) only if bleeding becomes an issue. --- ## 3. Post‑procedure diet after successful endoscopy * **Clear liquids** (water, clear broth, gelatin, clear juice) are the official benchmark for the first 4‑6 h. * If you are still a bit nauseated, **gentle ginger tea** (a small cup, no added sugar) is perfectly acceptable — ginger can actually help settle the stomach. * **Plain crackers** (saltine or “water crackers”) are also fine once you’re past the 4‑hour mark and can keep them down without any nausea. The key is to keep the volume low and the content bland; avoid acidic juices, dairy, or fatty foods until you’re sure your stomach tolerates liquids. So, after **4 h** you may try a sip of ginger tea; if that is tolerated, go ahead and have a few crackers. If you feel any nausea returns, stop, wait another hour, and try again. --- ## 4. Warning signs to call the team while you’re waiting | Sign | Why it matters | What to do | |------|----------------|------------| | **Vomiting** (especially projectile or bile‑stained) | Could indicate worsening obstruction or a developing perforation. | Call the nurse/physician immediately. | | **Fever > 38 °C (100.4 °F) or chills** | Possible infection or early cholangitis. | Call the team. | | **Sudden increase in abdominal pain or rigidity** | May signal perforation or ischemia. | Call/ask for urgent reassessment. | | **No passage of gas or stool for > 24 h** after the procedure | Suggests the obstruction persists. | Notify the team. | | **Shortness of breath, chest pain, or rapid heart rate** | Could be a pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, or an arrhythmia (especially with AF). | Call the nurse right away; they may call a rapid response. | | **Swelling, redness, or pain in the legs** | Possible deep‑vein thrombosis (DVT). | Report it; the team can order a duplex ultrasound. | | **Bleeding from the mouth, gums, or any new bruising** | May indicate over‑anticoagulation after warfarin is restarted. | Call the team; they may check your INR. | > **Bottom line:** Any new or worsening symptom—especially vomiting, fever, severe pain, or breathing difficulty—should be reported right away. --- ## 5. Follow‑up labs before discharge | Lab | When it’s done | Reason | |-----|----------------|--------| | **Basic metabolic panel (BMP)** – electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, glucose | **Within 24 h** of admission (often on the day of the procedure) | Checks kidney function (important for metformin & warfarin), electrolytes, and glucose control. | | **Complete blood count (CBC)** | Same as above | Looks for anemia (bleeding) or leukocytosis (infection). | | **INR** (if you’re on warfarin) | **After the procedure, before restarting warfarin** | Ensures your blood is back in the therapeutic range before you resume the drug. | | **Blood glucose** | Point‑of‑care checks **every 4–6 h** while you’re NPO, then **before discharge** if you’re eating | Keeps your diabetes controlled, especially after holding metformin. | | **Lactate** (only if there were any concern for ischemia) | Not routinely ordered unless the surgical team notices concerning signs. | Not expected to be needed here once the obstruction is resolved. | If all of those values are within acceptable limits (no significant bleeding, stable kidney function, INR ≈ 2‑3 when you restart warfarin), you will be cleared for discharge. Additional labs are ordered only if something changes (e.g., you develop a fever, you have a bleed, etc.). --- ## 6. Physical activity after you go home * **Day of discharge (or the day after if you’re still a little sore)** – Light **walking around the house** is encouraged. Aim for **10‑15 minutes**, a few times a day. This promotes circulation (prevents clots), improves lung ventilation, and helps your bowels “wake up.” * **Avoid**:
• Heavy lifting > 10 lb (including moving furniture, lifting laundry baskets, etc.) for **2 weeks**.
• Strenuous exercise, jogging, or sports for **at least 1 week** (or until your surgeon says it’s safe). * **Listen to your body** – If walking makes you feel dizzy, short‑of‑breath, or the pain returns, pause, sit down, and call the team. Otherwise, gradual activity is beneficial. --- ### Quick “cheat‑sheet” for you | Medication | Hold? | Restart | |------------|-------|---------| | Warfarin | Yes (night before) – LMWH bridge | Evening of procedure (if no bleed) | | Metformin | Yes (morning) | Same day when you tolerate food | | Lisinopril | Yes (morning) | Night of procedure or next morning | | Albuterol‑Ipratropium inhaler | No | Continue as usual | | Warning signs | Action | |----------------|--------| | Vomiting, fever, worsening pain, no gas, SOB, chest pain, leg swelling, new bruising | Call nurse/physician immediately (rapid response if needed) | | Post‑procedure diet | Timing | |---------------------|---------| | Clear liquids (water, broth, gelatin) | 4‑6 h after successful endoscopy | | Ginger tea or plain crackers | After 4 h if tolerated, otherwise wait until 6 h | | Activity after discharge | Guidance | |--------------------------|----------| | Light walking around house | Yes, start right away, 10‑15 min several times/day | | Heavy lifting > 10 lb | Avoid for 2 weeks | | Vigorous exercise | Hold for at least 1 week | --- **If anything else pops up—whether it’s a medication question, a new symptom, or just needing reassurance—please let me know right away.** I’m here to make sure you feel safe and fully informed every step of the way.

Past history includes ERCP with placement of a plastic biliary stent. This imaging finding, together with the clinical picture, confirms the diagnosis of foreign‑body small‑bowel obstruction caused by the migrated biliary stent.
